units.title: Unit 19 — Money
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 19. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Daily life · Money and personal finance
learningObjectives: Identify currencies, notes, coins and British English ways of referring to amounts of money.
Describe a bank account, cash, a cashpoint and being in credit.
Distinguish borrowing, owing, earning and paying money back.
Use waste money, save up for and afford accurately.
Discuss rents, deposits, landlords, fees and value for money.
Distinguish rent and hire, including the common options for cars.

items.example: The local currency is used in every shop.
items.note: A country's system of money, such as pounds or euros.

items.example: The invoice was paid in sterling.
items.note: The British currency; often used without an article.

items.example: A sandwich costs five pounds.
items.note: A unit of British currency; the plural is pounds.

items.example: The souvenir costs twenty dollars.
items.note: A unit of currency used in the United States and several other countries.

items.example: The museum ticket costs twelve euros.
items.note: The currency used in many European countries; plural euros.

items.example: I paid for the tickets with banknotes.
items.note: In British English, notes are paper money; American English often uses bills.

items.example: She found a coin under the sofa.
items.note: A small piece of metal used as money.

items.example: He keeps small coins in his pocket.
items.note: Plural of coin; contrast with notes.

items.example: The stamp costs eighty pence.
items.note: Pence is the ordinary plural used for amounts of money; one penny, two pence.

items.example: It costs fifty pence to make a copy.
items.note: Often said as fifty p in informal British English.

items.example: She gave the cashier a ten-pound note.
items.note: The unit stays singular in a compound modifier: ten-pound, not ten-pounds.

items.example: I found a twenty-euro note in my jacket.
items.note: Use singular euro before note in a compound modifier.

items.example: He dropped a fifty-pence piece on the floor.
items.note: A British coin worth fifty pence.

items.example: I need a one-pound coin for the trolley.
items.note: A compound modifier uses singular pound.

items.example: She opened a bank account when she started work.
items.note: An arrangement with a bank for keeping and managing money.

items.pt: com saldo positivo; com dinheiro na conta
items.example: My account is still in credit after paying the rent.
items.note: In credit means having money available in the account; contrast with being overdrawn.

items.example: There is a cashpoint outside the supermarket.
items.note: A British English word for an ATM; normally a machine for withdrawing cash.

items.example: Do you have any cash for the bus fare?
items.note: Money in notes or coins, rather than in a bank account or on a card.

items.example: I check my account before making a large purchase.
items.note: Check means look at the account details or balance.

items.example: You can check online to see whether the payment arrived.
items.note: Online is used as an adverb here.

items.example: Learning to manage your money can prevent debt.
items.note: Manage money means plan and control how it is used.

items.pt: sacar dinheiro; obter dinheiro em espécie
items.example: I stopped at a cashpoint to get cash.
items.note: A natural expression for withdrawing or obtaining physical money.

items.example: A student loan helped him pay for university.
items.note: A loan intended to cover education costs and usually repaid later.

items.example: They took out a loan to buy a car.
items.note: Money borrowed that must be repaid; often from a bank.

items.example: She applied for a bank loan last month.
items.note: A loan provided by a bank; explicitly practised in exercise 19.2.

items.example: The training course has high fees.
items.note: Amounts charged for services or education; a fee is normally countable.

items.example: The lawyer charges a fixed fee.
items.note: Money paid for a service; plural fees.

items.example: Buying things you never use can waste money.
items.note: Waste money means use it carelessly or without a useful result.

items.example: I still owe my friend twenty pounds.
items.note: Use owe somebody money or owe money to somebody.

items.example: I owe my sister some money for the tickets.
items.note: Owe describes an unpaid obligation, not the act of borrowing itself.

items.pt: pagar de volta; quitar uma dívida
items.example: I'll pay back the loan next year.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: pay the money back or pay it back.

items.pt: devolver o dinheiro; pagá-lo de volta
items.example: I borrowed twenty pounds and will pay it back tomorrow.
items.note: With a pronoun, put it between pay and back: pay it back, not pay back it.

items.pt: ganhar dinheiro pelo trabalho; receber como remuneração
items.example: She earns enough to cover her monthly expenses.
items.note: Earn means receive money for work, unlike borrow.

items.example: He earns money by working at weekends.
items.note: Earn money by doing a job; do not confuse earn with win.

items.example: They saved a reasonable amount in six months.
items.note: An amount is a quantity; reasonable here means fairly good or acceptable.

items.example: Write the amount on the payment form.
items.note: Use amount of money, not number of money.

items.example: Repairs could cost a large amount of money.
items.note: Use an amount of with uncountable nouns such as money.

items.pt: juntar dinheiro; economizar para comprar algo
items.example: I'm saving up for a new bicycle.
items.note: Save up for + something means put money aside for a future purchase.

items.pt: economizar para comprar; juntar dinheiro para
items.example: They're saving up for a holiday abroad.
items.note: Use the preposition for before the intended purchase or goal.

items.pt: ter condições financeiras de pagar; poder arcar com
items.example: We can't afford such an expensive hotel.
items.note: Afford is often used with can or can't; it means have enough money.

items.pt: não ter condições de; não poder pagar para
items.example: I can't afford to replace my laptop yet.
items.note: Use afford to + infinitive for an action; afford a noun for an object.

items.example: We found affordable accommodation near the station.
items.note: Usually uncountable in British English; places where people live or stay.

items.example: They decided to rent a flat with friends.
items.note: Rent means pay to use accommodation over a period of time.

items.example: The monthly rent includes water.
items.note: As a noun, rent is the payment; as a verb, it means pay to use something.

items.example: We pay rent at the start of each month.
items.note: A common verb–noun combination: pay rent.

items.example: The deposit was equal to one month's rent.
items.note: The possessive indicates a period: one month's rent.

items.example: We got the deposit back after moving out.
items.note: In a rental context, money held as security and often returned later.

items.example: We had to pay a deposit before moving in.
items.note: A deposit is usually paid in advance.

items.example: They got their deposit back when the lease ended.
items.note: The money is returned if the relevant conditions are met.

items.example: This budget hotel is good value for money.
items.note: Good value for money means the quality is good for the price paid.

items.pt: proprietário que aluga um imóvel; locador
items.example: Our landlord repairs things quickly.
items.note: A person who owns property and rents it to others.

items.example: The hotel doesn't charge for breakfast.
items.note: Charge somebody an amount or charge for a service.

items.example: Some banks charge for international transfers.
items.note: Use charge for + service or product; charge somebody + an amount.

items.example: We hired a bike for the afternoon.
items.note: In British English, hire is common for short-term use; rent often suggests longer periods.

items.example: We hired a car to explore the coast.
items.note: Both hire a car and rent a car are natural in British English.

items.example: They rented a car at the airport.
items.note: Rent and hire are both used for cars; rent is particularly common in American English.

units.title: Unit 20 — Health
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 20. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Daily life · Symptoms, pain and illnesses
learningObjectives: Describe everyday symptoms and common self-care actions using natural British English.
Choose articles correctly in a cough, a sore throat, a temperature, flu and backache.
Distinguish ache, pain, hurt and painful, including common body-part combinations.
Use the patterns suffer from, have an operation and go into hospital.
Recognise serious illnesses, body organs and the role of a surgeon.
Explain the distinction between disease and illness and use common medical collocations.

items.pt: qual é o problema?; o que houve?
items.example: You look uncomfortable; what's the matter?
items.note: A common question about what is wrong; used when somebody seems ill or upset.

items.example: I've got a sore throat and don't want to talk.
items.note: Use a sore throat when describing a symptom; sore means painful.

items.example: She has a sore throat after singing all night.
items.note: A common expression with have or have got and the article a.

items.example: The child has a temperature and should rest.
items.note: Have a temperature often means have a fever, not merely have body temperature.

items.example: He has a temperature, so he's staying at home.
items.note: British English expression; use a before temperature in this sense.

items.example: She missed work because she had flu.
items.note: British English commonly says have flu with no article.

items.example: I stayed at home because I had flu.
items.note: In British English, typically no article; American English often says have the flu.

items.example: If your symptoms get worse, see a doctor.
items.note: See a doctor means visit a medical professional for advice or treatment.

items.example: I cut my hand while cooking.
items.note: The verb has the same form in the present, past and past participle.

items.pt: cortar o braço; fazer um corte no braço
items.example: Be careful not to cut your arm on the broken glass.
items.note: An ordinary verb–object pattern for a cut or injury.

items.example: Small cuts may bleed for a short time.
items.note: Irregular verb: bleed, bled, bled.

items.example: The wound is bleeding, so she needs a bandage.
items.note: Present participle of bleed; note the double e.

items.example: The nurse put a bandage around his ankle.
items.note: A strip or covering used to protect an injury.

items.pt: colocar uma bandagem em volta de
items.example: Put a bandage around the injured arm.
items.note: Around and round are both possible; put takes the same form in the past.

items.example: His cough got worse during the night.
items.note: As a noun, say a cough; the verb is cough.

items.example: I've had a cough since Monday.
items.note: Use a cough with an article when naming this symptom.

items.example: I'll go to the chemist for some medicine.
items.note: British English: the chemist can mean the pharmacy or the pharmacist.

items.example: This medicine must be kept away from heat.
items.note: Medicine is generally uncountable when it means a substance used to treat illness.

items.pt: remédio para tosse; xarope para tosse
items.example: The pharmacist recommended some cough medicine.
items.note: A type of medicine for coughing; generally uncountable.

items.example: She had a headache after a long day.
items.note: A headache is countable; use a headache.

items.example: I have a headache and need a quiet room.
items.note: Use have or have got with a headache.

items.example: Take one tablet with a glass of water.
items.note: A small solid dose of medicine; often called a pill.

items.example: These tablets should be taken with food.
items.note: Countable plural of tablet; often interchangeable with pills.

items.example: She swallowed the pill with water.
items.note: A small solid form of medicine; countable.

items.example: The doctor prescribed pills for the pain.
items.note: Plural of pill; often similar in meaning to tablets.

items.example: The pain was worse when he moved his leg.
items.note: Pain may be countable or uncountable depending on context.

items.example: I feel sick after that long bus journey.
items.note: British English: feel sick often means feel as though you may vomit.

items.pt: dor persistente; doer de forma contínua
items.example: My shoulders ache after carrying heavy bags.
items.note: As a verb, ache describes a dull or continuing pain.

items.example: My legs were aching after the walk.
items.note: The -ing form of ache describes pain that continues.

items.pt: dor de estômago; dor de barriga
items.example: He stayed home because of stomach ache.
items.note: In British English, often uncountable as stomach ache; a stomach ache is also used.

items.example: She gets backache after sitting all day.
items.note: Usually uncountable in British English; write backache as one word.

items.example: I have backache after moving the furniture.
items.note: Typically no article with backache in British English.

items.example: He suffers from frequent migraines.
items.note: Use suffer from + illness, problem or pain that someone experiences.

items.example: My aunt suffers from backache.
items.note: An example of suffer from followed by an uncountable symptom.

items.example: I've got a pain in my shoulder after training.
items.note: Use a pain in + body part when describing a localised pain.

items.example: My knee hurts when I bend it.
items.note: Hurt can mean be painful or cause pain; past tense is hurt.

items.example: It hurts to walk on my injured foot.
items.note: Third-person singular of hurt; also used after it.

items.example: The treatment was uncomfortable but not painful.
items.note: An adjective describing something that causes pain.

items.example: He recovered after a serious illness.
items.note: A serious illness is a severe health problem.

items.example: She returned to work after a long illness.
items.note: Illness can describe both a health problem and the period when someone is ill.

items.example: Some diseases affect particular organs.
items.note: Disease often refers to a specific medical condition, rather than a period of illness.

items.example: Regular exercise can help reduce the risk of heart disease.
items.note: Disease is natural for a specific condition or group of conditions.

items.example: Mental illness can affect people of any age.
items.note: Illness is suitable for mental health conditions; disease is not always interchangeable.

items.pt: ser internado em um hospital; ir para o hospital
items.example: She had to go into hospital for treatment.
items.note: British English often omits the with hospital when referring to receiving medical care.

items.example: The patient spoke to the surgeon before the procedure.
items.note: A person receiving medical treatment or care.

items.example: My grandfather had an operation last year.
items.note: A medical procedure performed by surgeons; often have an operation.

items.pt: passar por uma operação; fazer uma cirurgia
items.example: She's going to have an operation on her knee.
items.note: Use have an operation when a patient undergoes surgery.

items.example: He needed surgery after the accident.
items.note: In the medical procedure sense, surgery is normally uncountable.

items.example: The surgeon explained what would happen next.
items.note: A doctor trained to perform operations.

items.example: The surgeon will perform an operation tomorrow.
items.note: The answer key pairs surgeon with operation; patients have operations and surgeons perform them.

items.example: The left lung is slightly smaller than the right.
items.note: One of the organs used for breathing.

items.example: The lungs take oxygen into the body.
items.note: Plural of lung; two main breathing organs.

items.example: Smoking increases the risk of lung cancer.
items.note: A serious disease affecting the lungs; normally uncountable.

items.example: Research has improved some cancer treatments.
items.note: A disease involving abnormal cell growth; generally uncountable as a condition.

items.example: The heart pumps blood around the body.
items.note: An organ that pumps blood through the body.

items.example: He recovered after a heart attack.
items.note: A sudden medical emergency affecting the heart; a heart attack is countable.

items.example: Hepatitis affects the liver.
items.note: A disease involving inflammation of the liver; normally no article.

items.example: The liver is an important organ.
items.note: An organ involved in many processes including filtering substances from the blood.
